title: Customs Tariff Amendment (Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership Implementation) Bill 2018
short_title: Customs Tariff Amendment (Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership Implementation) Bill 2018

summary.attribution: Written by a model from the explanatory memorandum; not the record
sentences: This bill would cut customs duties on goods imported from countries that are part of the TPP-11 trade deal.
It would add new preferential duty rates and a new schedule for alcohol, tobacco and fuel products to the Customs Tariff Act 1995.
The government estimates implementing the TPP-11 would not add extra cost beyond the $195 million reduction in customs duty collections already budgeted.
changes: Provide preferential customs duty rates for TPP-11 originating goods.
Insert a new schedule for excise-equivalent duties on alcohol, tobacco and fuel products.
Amend concessional items in Schedule 4 to maintain duty rates in line with the TPP-11.
summary.affected: Importers of goods from TPP-11 countries.

speeches.speaker: Steven Ciobo
speeches.brief: The Customs Tariff Amendment (Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership Implementation) Bill 2018 reduces customs duties on TPP originating goods, with most removed upon entry into force and the rest phased out over four years, while maintaining excise-equivalent duties for consistency with domestic goods. Andrew Robb and Department of Foreign Affairs and Trade staff were thanked for their work.

speeches.speaker: Jason Clare
speeches.brief: Labor will support the CPTPP implementation bills but opposes the government's waiver of labour market testing for six countries and the inclusion of investor-state dispute settlement (ISDS) clauses; if elected, Labor will seek to remove ISDS, reinstate labour market testing, require independent economic assessments of all trade deals, and strengthen parliamentary scrutiny.

speeches.speaker: Madeleine King
speeches.brief: The speaker supported the amendments to the CPTPP implementation bills proposed by the member for Blaxland, arguing for free trade that includes strong labour standards, environmental protections, and transparency, while opposing investor-state dispute settlement provisions and committing to restore labour market testing if Labor is elected.

speeches.speaker: Mark Coulton
speeches.brief: The TPP-11 will eliminate over 98% of tariffs on Australian exports to 11 Asia-Pacific countries with a combined GDP of $13.8 trillion and 500 million consumers, delivering specific benefits such as the elimination of Canadian beef tariffs (currently 26.5%) within five years and Mexican beef tariffs (up to 25%) within ten years. The speaker argued the agreement strengthens Australia’s free trade network, provides new opportunities for agricultural and service exporters, and does not weaken Australian labour, skills or regulatory standards.

speeches.speaker: David Gillespie
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the TPP-11 will eliminate tariffs with 11 countries worth $13.8 trillion combined GDP, boost exports for farmers, manufacturers, and service providers, and increase Australia's net national income by $15.5 billion by 2030.

speeches.speaker: Chris Hayes
speeches.brief: Labor supported the Customs Amendment and Customs Tariff Amendment bills implementing the Comprehensive and Progressive Agreement for Trans-Pacific Partnership, along with the shadow trade minister's amendment, citing the agreement's side agreements on human rights, labour rights and the environment. The party raised concerns about investor-state dispute provisions—noting only Canada would newly be subject to them—and argued for transitional arrangements and investment in education and TAFE to keep Australian workers competitive.

speeches.speaker: Steven Ciobo
speeches.brief: The speaker argued for the swift passage of the TPP-11 implementing bills, stating the agreement would eliminate 98% of tariffs, deliver a $15.6 billion net annual benefit to national income by 2030, and give Australian beef exporters a 13 percentage point tariff advantage over US competitors in Japan within two years.

speeches.speaker: Steven Ciobo
speeches.brief: The speaker argued that the TPP-11 trade deal is right for Australia, citing market access benefits for regional farmers and dismissing claims about labour migration loopholes as "completely and utterly absurd." They noted that the only waiver is on domestic advertising for labour market testing, a measure previously implemented by the Labor Party, and that the deal will drive economic growth, exports and jobs.
